titre: Les Fleurs du mal (The Flowers of Evil) Was Never Banned: Six Poems Were
accroche: In 1857, the Seine criminal court convicts Baudelaire over six poems; it will take a 1946 law for the Cour de cassation (France's supreme court) to wipe the conviction out in 1949.
contenu_vulgarise:
People say that *Les Fleurs du mal* (*The Flowers of Evil*) was banned. It is both true and false: the 1857 conviction cut six poems from the collection, not the entire collection.

## August 1857

The book comes out in late June 1857, from Poulet-Malassis and De Broise. It is pulled from sale on July 17. On August 20, the “tribunal correctionnel” (criminal court) of the Seine (sixth chamber) convicts Baudelaire of “outrage à la morale publique” (outrage to public morality): a fine of 300 francs, 100 francs for each of his two publishers, and the suppression of six pieces, “Les Bijoux” (“The Jewels”), “Le Léthé” (“Lethe”), “À celle qui est trop gaie” (“To Her Who Is Too Joyful”), “Lesbos,” “Femmes damnées” (“Women Doomed”) and “Les Métamorphoses du vampire” (“The Vampire's Metamorphoses”). The “substitut du procureur impérial” (deputy imperial prosecutor) is Ernest Pinard, who had argued the case against *Madame Bovary* a few months earlier. Baudelaire will get his fine reduced to 50 francs, after an appeal to the empress.

It is therefore the court that singles out the six poems: it leaves the rest of the collection aside. The prosecution also charged outrage to religious morality, but, according to the Ministry of Justice's account, only outrage to public morality is upheld against him.

## Ninety-Two Years Later

To overturn a conviction for “outrage aux bonnes mœurs” (offense against public decency), a procedure was needed that did not exist. Parliament created it in 1946, at the initiative of the Communist deputy Georges Cogniot, through a single article passed without opposition: a law allows a review of convictions of literary works to be requested, on petition from the “Société des gens de lettres” (Society of Men of Letters). Baudelaire's request for review is the first application of this law.

On May 31, 1949, after twelve days of deliberation, the “chambre criminelle” (criminal chamber) of the “Cour de cassation” (France's supreme court) wipes out the 1857 conviction: it clears the memory of Baudelaire and of his two publishers, Poulet-Malassis and De Broise.

## What This Shifts

French law in 1857 does not punish a book: it punishes poems, and an express law is needed, ninety-two years later, for justice to undo what it has done. And what it rehabilitates in 1949 is the memory of the author and of his publishers, named explicitly in the decision: Charles Baudelaire, Auguste Poulet-Malassis and Eugène de Broise. Irony would have it that the magistrate who prosecuted in 1857, Ernest Pinard, also went after *Madame Bovary* a few months earlier.

repere.texte: On August 20, 1857, the Seine criminal court sentences Baudelaire to a fine of 300 francs and orders the suppression of six poems from Les Fleurs du mal; on May 31, 1949, the criminal chamber of the Cour de cassation wipes out this conviction.
repere.source: Ministry of Justice, “Quand les fleurs faillirent faner…” (When the Flowers Nearly Withered), July 24, 2007

carte.punch: Les Fleurs du mal was never banned: six poems were, in 1857.
carte.idee: The Seine court convicts Baudelaire on August 20, 1857, and orders the suppression of six pieces. It will take a 1946 law and a ruling of May 31, 1949 for the Cour de cassation to wipe the conviction out.

quiz.question: What exactly does the court condemn in August 1857?
choix: Six poems from the collection, cut from the edition
The entire collection, pulled from sale with no reprieve
Only the publishers, Baudelaire being acquitted
Only the poems judged religiously blasphemous
quiz.explication: The court orders the suppression of six pieces and upholds outrage to public morality; it does not strike the collection as a whole.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Cour de cassation do on May 31, 1949?
choix: It authorizes a new edition but upholds the 1857 conviction
It wipes out the conviction, after a 1946 law allowing review
It rewrites the judgment, condemning only Lesbos
It hands down the decision at the request of Baudelaire's family
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A 1946 law allows review of convictions of literary works, on petition from the Société des gens de lettres; Baudelaire is its first beneficiary.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who prosecutes Baudelaire in 1857, and what had he done a few months earlier?
choix: Ernest Pinard, who had also prosecuted Madame Bovary
Georges Cogniot, future deputy behind the 1946 law
Eugène de Broise, one of the two convicted publishers
Auguste Poulet-Malassis, the other convicted publisher
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The deputy imperial prosecutor Ernest Pinard had prosecuted Flaubert's Madame Bovary a few months earlier, the entry says.
